corrected_value.title: Having Control Over and Above Situations: The Influence of Elevated Viewpoints on Risk Taking
corrected_value.title_o: Having Control Over and Above Situations: The Influence of Elevated Viewpoints on Risk Taking

decisions.quote:
In this post, we report our attempt to replicate a study in a recently published
Journal of Marketing Research
(
JMR
) article entitled, “Having Control Over and Above Situations: The Influence of Elevated Viewpoints on Risk Taking” (
.htm
). The article’s abstract summarizes the key result: “consumers’ views of scenery from a high physical elevation induce an illusory source of control, which in turn intensifies risk taking.”
Four of the article’s seven studies were conducted on MTurk. We tried to replicate Study 1b because it has the smallest reported
p
-value of the four (p = .016). This study (N = 203) found that “people exposed to high-elevation sceneries [were] more willing to purchase new products than people exposed to low-elevation images” (p. 56).
decisions.reason: The primary source explicitly states that it replicates Study 1b of the recently published Journal of Marketing Research article entitled 'Having Control Over and Above Situations: The Influence of Elevated Viewpoints on Risk Taking'. While the scraped blog text only hyperlinked the article without printing the author surname, year, or DOI in plain text (causing the blind coding to have only the title and leaving pairing unresolved), both blind target 0 and shipped row 2721 (Jami, 2019, 10.1177/0022243718813544) identify the exact same tested original paper.

decisions.quote: In sum, using three times the sample size as the original study, we find no evidence that being exposed to an elevated vertical position increases risk taking, at least when risk is operationalized as the likelihood of purchasing new products.
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Jami (2019) Study 1b, the replicating authors state an explicit overall verdict in the Conclusions section that using three times the original sample size (N = 603 vs. N = 203), they find no evidence that exposure to an elevated vertical position increases risk taking (M_HIGH = 3.67 vs. M_LOW = 3.64, p = .802, d = .02). Both shipped and blind codings correctly recorded 'failed'.

decisions.quote:
In the preregistered replication (
https://aspredicted.org/9zw6i.pdf
), we used the same instructions, procedures, images, questions, and participant population as in the original study. Except for sample size – we sought to get three times the original sample size – the only difference we are aware of between our study and the original is that our formatting of the scenery questions on Qualtrics was slightly different from the original author’s formatting (see this
.pdf
for an example).
decisions.reason: The study collected new survey data from 603 MTurk participants using the original study's materials and procedures to re-test the published finding from Study 1b of Jami (2019). Both shipped and blind codings correctly classify the record type as 'replication'.

Independent current primary finding and citation context: Blog explicitly names the exact JMR elevated-viewpoints title, selects Study1b (N203, p=.016), describes high versus low images and new-product purchasing, and reports its own attempted test. Row2721 original receipt supplies Jami2019 metadata matching that title. The actual original identity printed or uniquely described in the current source matches the retained row or its separately source-supported correction; pairing alone is not proof. Primary scrape lacks printed author/year/DOI fields; these remain empty in original/current target payload. Original body and hyperlink destination were not independently examined. This disposition concerns only the bound current target; other descendants retain separate dispositions. No new original-field error, report/cohort equivalence or outcome is inferred. Old raw-coding blanks and nonliteral strings remain unchanged; independent literal primary proof is supplied here.
